meta.name: CCNP ENCOR 350-401
meta.notes: [encor batch 1: 14 scenario rewrites] [encor batch 2: 14 scenario rewrites] [encor batch 3 (final): 12 scenario rewrites. ENCOR fully rewritten.]

questions.question: Cisco SD-Access overlay control plane separates a device's IDENTITY (its IPv4/IPv6 address as seen by apps) from its LOCATION (the routing locator — the fabric edge node attached to). The mapping is kept in a control-plane database. Endpoints can move between fabric edges without renumbering. Which protocol?
options: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) — separates EID (identity) from RLOC (locator); SD-Access control plane
Replaces OSPF — false; LISP is overlay control plane, OSPF underneath as underlay IGP
Wireless standard — false; LISP is an L3 overlay control protocol
Firewall protocol — false; LISP is for routing/mobility, not packet filtering
questions.explanation: In SD-Access, LISP provides the control plane. EIDs are IP/MAC addresses of endpoints; RLOCs are the tunnel endpoints (fabric edges). LISP Map-Server/Resolver manages the mapping database for endpoint mobility.

questions.question: A data centre needs Layer-2 reachability across racks AND beyond the 4094 VLAN limit. The team picks an L2-over-L3 overlay that encapsulates Ethernet frames in UDP (port 4789), uses a 24-bit VNI (~16M segments), and is routed by the underlay. Which?
options: A routing protocol — wrong category
An encryption standard — wrong category
A 2-VLAN extension only — false; VXLAN has 16M VNIs
VXLAN — Virtual eXtensible LAN: L2-over-L3 overlay, UDP/4789, 24-bit VNI (~16M segments), routed by IP underlay
questions.explanation: VXLAN solves VLAN scalability in data centers and SD-Access. Each VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier) is equivalent to a VLAN but allows 16M overlays. VXLAN EVPN uses BGP for control plane.

questions.question: Cisco BGP best-path selection is ORDERED — each tie-breaker only kicks in if the previous didn't decide. The FIRST three checks are: (1) Weight (Cisco-proprietary, router-local, higher wins), (2) Local Preference (advertised inside AS via iBGP, higher wins), (3) Locally-originated (`network`, `aggregate`, `redistribute` > learned). Which is the canonical first-three?
options: Weight (Cisco-proprietary, router-local, higher wins); Local Preference (intra-AS via iBGP, higher wins); Locally-originated (network / aggregate / redistribute over learned)
Metric → weight → local preference — wrong order
Local preference only — incomplete
AS path only — wrong; AS path comes LATER (after origin type and several others)
questions.explanation: BGP bestpath mnemonic: 'We Love Oranges As Oranges Mean Pure Refreshment' (Weight, Local Pref, Locally originated, AS Path, Origin, MED, eBGP>iBGP, IGP metric, Router ID). Higher Weight/Local Pref preferred. highest wins) → Local Preference (highest wins) → Locally originated → AS Path length (shortest wins) → Origin → MED → eBGP > iBGP → IGP metric

questions.question: An MPLS SP wants to route GOLD-tier customer traffic along a specific path satisfying bandwidth + latency constraints, not just the IGP shortest. RSVP-TE signals LSPs with explicit-path + bandwidth requirements. Which feature?
options: MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) — signalled LSPs with bandwidth + explicit-path constraints via RSVP-TE; overrides IGP shortest
Encrypts MPLS — wrong concern (security, not path control)
BGP extension — wrong category
QoS mechanism — TE is path control, QoS is per-class queuing (separate)
questions.explanation: MPLS-TE uses RSVP-TE to signal LSPs with bandwidth reservations. Allows routing around congested links even if IGP shortest path goes through them. Useful for WAN optimization and SLA guarantees.

questions.question: An AS with 50 iBGP speakers naively needs 50×49/2 = 1225 iBGP sessions (full mesh) because iBGP routes are NOT re-advertised to other iBGP peers. A feature designates ROUTE REFLECTORS that re-advertise iBGP routes to their CLIENTS, eliminating the n² mesh. Which describes RR usage?
options: Only for IPv6 — false
Only for eBGP — false; RR is iBGP scaling
Required when iBGP full-mesh becomes impractical (n²); RR re-advertises iBGP routes to its clients; cluster-id + originator-id prevent loops
Needed in every BGP deployment — false; small ASes can run full-mesh iBGP
questions.explanation: iBGP prevents routing loops with split-horizon (don't re-advertise iBGP to iBGP). RR exception: clients can receive and accept routes from RR. Cluster ID prevents loops between multiple RRs.

questions.question: An OSPF ABR sits between Area 0 and a non-backbone area. It learns Type 1/2 LSAs intra-area, then generates a SUMMARY LSA (carrying network + mask + metric) to advertise the prefix into OTHER areas. Receivers of this LSA route by metric. Which LSA Type and originator?
options: Type 3 Summary LSA — generated by ABRs to advertise INTER-AREA prefixes; carries network + mask + cost
Type 4 ASBR-Summary — describes ASBR location, not inter-area prefixes
Type 1 Router LSA from every router — INTRA-area, not inter-area
Type 5 External — describes external redistributed routes, not inter-area
questions.explanation: LSA types: 1=Router (all routers), 2=Network (DR), 3=Summary/Network (ABR, inter-area), 4=ASBR Summary (ABR), 5=External (ASBR, external routes), 7=NSSA external. ABR generates 3/4; ASBR generates 5/7.

questions.question: Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) has FOUR architectural roles. (A) vManage = single-pane orchestration / GUI / API. (B) vSmart = control plane (overlay routes + policy enforcement). (C) vBond = onboarding / NAT-traversal helper. (D) WAN-edge routers = data plane. Which mapping is correct?
options: A hardware router platform — false; SD-Access has hardware but Viptela is the SDN role-split
vManage = management plane GUI; vSmart = control plane (routes + policy); vBond = orchestration / NAT traversal; WAN-edge routers carry the data plane
Just a CPE — false; the architecture is a multi-controller system
Identical names — false
questions.explanation: SD-WAN control plane: vSmart distributes OMP (Overlay Management Protocol) routes and policies. vBond performs initial authentication and NAT traversal. vManage provides GUI management. Data plane uses IPsec overlays.

questions.question: Two link-state IGPs compared: (A) OSPF — runs over IP (protocol 89), area-numbered hierarchically (Area 0 + non-backbone), IPv4-only LSAs (OSPFv2) or IPv6-only LSAs (OSPFv3 per AF). (B) IS-IS — runs DIRECTLY ON LAYER 2 (CLNS), areas numbered Level-1 / Level-2, single process supports IPv4 AND IPv6. Which describes IS-IS?
options: IS-IS uses areas — partially true but not the distinguishing feature
IS-IS is IPv4-only — false; IS-IS supports both natively
IS-IS = link-state IGP running directly on L2 (CLNS, not over IP); L1/L2 area hierarchy; natively supports IPv4 + IPv6 in one process; common in SP backbones
IS-IS only for large networks — context-dependent, not a definition
questions.explanation: IS-IS runs over Layer 2 (Clnp/Data Link) not IP — immune to IP misconfiguration attacks. Level 1 = intra-area, Level 2 = backbone. No /8 area number limit like OSPF. Widely used by ISPs (Tier 1/2).

questions.question: DMVPN has THREE phases. (Phase 1) hub-to-spoke ONLY (spokes can't talk directly). (Phase 2) DYNAMIC spoke-to-spoke tunnels via NHRP — spoke A discovers B's NBMA address and builds a direct GRE tunnel; hub stays in the routing path. (Phase 3) NHRP summarisation + redirects so the data plane goes spoke-to-spoke immediately. Which describes the phases?
options: Only for large enterprises — context-dependent
Static VPN — false; DMVPN is dynamic
Phase 1 hub-only; Phase 2 dynamic spoke-to-spoke via NHRP; Phase 3 NHRP summarisation + redirect for direct data-plane
Replacement for MPLS — different shape; DMVPN is an overlay over public internet, MPLS is provider-managed
questions.explanation: DMVPN uses mGRE + NHRP + IPsec. Hub-spoke-spoke communication: spoke queries NHRP for other spoke's RLOC, builds direct tunnel. Phase 2: full spoke-to-spoke. Phase 3: adds NHRP redirect for scalability.

questions.question: QoS markings use the DSCP field (6 bits in the IP TOS/Traffic-Class byte → 64 values). Important markings: EF (46) for VoIP, AF31/AF41 for video, CS6 (48) for network control, CS5 for IP-precedence interop with legacy 3-bit IP-Prec values. Which describes DSCP and key markings?
options: DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point): 6-bit IP-header field (64 values); EF (46) voice, AF31/AF41 video, CS6 (48) network control, CS5/CS6 etc. for IP-precedence interop
Voice-only markings — false; DSCP covers all traffic classes
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: DSCP markings enable per-hop QoS behavior. EF (Expedited Forwarding) for VoIP — strict priority queue. AF classes (AF11-AF43) for business-critical apps. Markings should be set as close to source as possible. 6-bit field in IP header. Key values: EF (46) = VoIP/real-time, AF41 (34) = video conferencing, AF21 (18) = critical data, CS3 (24) = call signaling, default/BE (0) = best effort

questions.question: An OSPF design has a non-backbone Area 5 attached only to Area 2 (no direct Area-0 link). OSPF rules require every non-backbone area to TOUCH Area 0. A logical construct lets the area's ABR reach Area 0 ACROSS a transit area without a real circuit. Which?
options: OSPF virtual link — connects a non-backbone area to Area 0 through a transit area; logical, not a real circuit
OSPF stub area — different feature (LSA filtering)
GRE tunnel over OSPF — works at the data plane but isn't the OSPF-internal virtual link
Route redistribution — different concern (cross-protocol)
questions.explanation: Virtual links are used when an area can't directly connect to Area 0 (temporary fix during network design). Transit area must not be stub. Configure on both ABRs: 'area X virtual-link [router-id-of-other-ABR]'.

questions.question: EIGRP's loop-free pre-computed alternative path requires the Feasibility Condition: a candidate's ADVERTISED DISTANCE (RD = neighbor's metric to the destination) must be LESS than the current successor's FEASIBLE DISTANCE (FD = my best metric). The path passing this check is the Feasible Successor and installs INSTANTLY on successor failure. Which describes FC + FS?
options: (empty) — no
Any backup route — false; the FC must hold (RD < FD)
A loop-free backup route satisfying the Feasibility Condition (RD < successor's FD); installs immediately on successor failure — sub-second EIGRP convergence
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: Feasibility Condition: neighbor's AD < local FD. If met, that route is a Feasible Successor (FS). EIGRP instantly switches to FS on failure (active state avoided). Without FS, EIGRP queries neighbors (active state).

questions.question: Cisco ACI is a data-centre SDN solution with: APIC controller (HA cluster), spine-leaf physical fabric, INTENT-BASED policy via 'EPG' (Endpoint Group) + CONTRACTS, abstract / declarative model. Application teams define policies; the fabric implements them across physical + virtual workloads. Which describes ACI?
options: (empty) — no
Cisco ACI = data-centre SDN with APIC controller, spine-leaf fabric, intent-based EPG + contract policy model
(empty) — no
A routing protocol — false; ACI is an SDN solution
questions.explanation: ACI: APIC controller + Nexus 9000 spine/leaf. Policy model: Tenant → Application Profile → EPG (Endpoint Group). Contracts define allowed communication between EPGs. Automates data center provisioning via REST API.

questions.question: OSPF Hello = 10 s, BGP keepalive = 60 s — both too slow for sub-second failover. A LIGHTWEIGHT companion protocol exchanges very-frequent (e.g., 50 ms) Hellos between two endpoints; on failure it INSTANTLY notifies the routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, static) to converge. Which protocol?
options: (empty) — no
(empty) — no
BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) — lightweight L3 protocol with sub-second timers; signals failure to routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, static); fast reroute
A routing protocol — BFD complements routing protocols rather than being one
questions.explanation: BFD sends hellos every 50-300ms (vs OSPF 10s default). Detects link failures in <1 second. Works with: OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, IS-IS, static routes. Must be enabled on both ends. Uses UDP port 3784/3785.

questions.question: Two VXLAN data-plane modes: (A) FLOOD-AND-LEARN — VTEPs discover MACs via BUM traffic flooded across the underlay multicast; no control plane awareness; scalability issues at large fabric. (B) MP-BGP EVPN — VTEPs advertise MAC + IP bindings in BGP control plane; no flooding required. Which mapping?
options: Identical — false
(empty) — no
Flood-and-learn = MAC discovery via data-plane BUM flooding (legacy Ethernet model, scale issues); EVPN = MP-BGP control plane carries MAC + IP advertisements (no flood, modern scalable)
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: VXLAN with EVPN (Type 2 routes: MAC/IP; Type 3: multicast/BUM) uses BGP to distribute endpoint info before packets arrive. Eliminates flood-and-learn scalability issues. Standard for modern data center fabrics.

questions.question: In BGP routing, a ROUTE LEAK is when a router advertises routes RECEIVED from one peer to ANOTHER peer in violation of routing policy. The classic example: a customer multi-homed to ISP-A and ISP-B advertises ISP-A's full table to ISP-B, causing transit they're not supposed to provide. Prevention: prefix lists + AS-PATH filters + BGP RPKI for origin validation. Which describes route leak?
options: A BGP router advertising routes from one peer to another in violation of policy (e.g., customer transiting between ISPs); prevented by prefix-lists, AS-PATH filters, RPKI / ROAs
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
Physical fibre cut — wrong category
questions.explanation: Route leaks cause internet outages (e.g., 2019 Cloudflare incident). Prevention: strict outbound filters, BGP communities to tag routes, RPKI/ROA validation (filters invalid origin ASNs), and IRR-based filters.

questions.question: An MPLS-enabled core has hundreds of LSRs forwarding packets by label-swapping. Each LSR must learn which label its UPSTREAM neighbour uses for a given FEC. Cisco runs a control protocol on TCP 646 to advertise label-to-FEC bindings between LSRs. Which protocol?
options: Bandwidth reservation — that's RSVP-TE, different
LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) — distributes label-to-FEC bindings between LSRs (TCP/UDP 646); enables MPLS forwarding
Encryption — wrong category
Routing protocol — LDP rides on top of an IGP, isn't itself one
questions.explanation: LDP assigns local labels to IP prefixes and exchanges them with neighbors. Ingress router pushes label; transit routers swap labels; egress pops label. LSPs follow IGP shortest path. Alternative: RSVP-TE for TE. distributes label bindings between MPLS-enabled routers, building the Label Forwarding Information Base (LFIB) used for label-based packet forwarding.

questions.question: Cisco's central INTENT-BASED NETWORKING controller for ENTERPRISE network management. Provides: Design (templates), Provisioning (push to onboarded devices), Assurance (ML-based health analytics), Policy (group-based segmentation via SGTs). Renamed Catalyst Center in 2024. Which product?
options: Cisco DNA Center (now Catalyst Center) — central IBN controller: Design, Provision, Assurance, Policy
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
Hardware appliance only — false; DNA Center / Catalyst Center is the software platform
questions.explanation: DNA Center automates campus network lifecycle: design (IP addressing, VLANs), policy (micro-segmentation via SGTs), provision (zero-touch deployment), assurance (AI-driven troubleshooting using network telemetry).

questions.question: Cisco's MODERN NetFlow lets the operator CHOOSE which packet fields to use as flow keys (e.g., src IP + dst IP + port + ToS + AS number) and which fields to collect (interfaces, byte counts, TCP flags, AS path). Operators tune flow caches per use-case. Which feature?
options: Flexible NetFlow — operator-defined key + non-key fields per flow cache; supersedes classic 5-tuple NetFlow v5/v9
Source IP only — false; flexible NetFlow collects many fields
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: NetFlow/IPFIX captures flow metadata (not payload). Key fields: src/dst IP, src/dst port, protocol, bytes, packets, timestamps. Used for capacity planning, security analysis (detect DDoS, data exfiltration) and billing.

questions.question: Cisco TrustSec assigns a 16-bit GROUP TAG to each authenticated endpoint at the point of authentication (via ISE). The tag propagates with the packet inline (Cisco metadata header) or via SXP (peer-to-peer). Policy enforcement compares src + dst tags at the egress device against a permissions matrix. What is this architecture?
options: (empty) — no

TrustSec = SGT (Scalable Group Tag) based architecture: ISE assigns SGT at auth; tags propagate inline or via SXP; policy enforcement at egress devices using SGT-based ACL matrix; decouples policy from IP / VLAN
(empty) — no
VPN technology — false; TrustSec is identity-based policy, not VPN
questions.explanation: TrustSec assigns SGTs via 802.1X/ISE authentication. SGTs are carried in Ethernet headers (CMD tag) or VXLAN headers across the fabric. Policies (SGACLs) defined in ISE are enforced at fabric edges.

questions.question: In DMVPN Phase 2 / 3, a SPOKE wants to build a tunnel directly to ANOTHER spoke (skipping the hub). It needs to RESOLVE the other spoke's PUBLIC (NBMA / underlay) IP from the spoke's overlay tunnel IP. The hub maintains a dynamic mapping table; spokes query it on demand via a specific protocol. Which?
options: (empty) — no
A routing protocol — wrong category
(empty) — no
NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol) — resolves overlay tunnel IP → underlay NBMA IP via the hub's mapping table; enables dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels
questions.explanation: NHRP is the 'phone book' for DMVPN. Hubs are NHS (Next Hop Servers); spokes register their IP. When spoke A needs to reach spoke B, it queries NHS, gets B's NBMA address, and builds a direct IPsec/GRE tunnel. allows spoke routers to dynamically discover the physical IP (NBMA address) of other spokes through the hub, enabling direct spoke-to-spoke tunnels in DMVPN Phase 2/3.

questions.question: Cisco ships THREE distinct OS lineages. (A) Modular IOS for enterprise routers/switches (ASR, ISR, Cat9k). (B) Carrier-grade HA OS for SP edge (ASR9k / NCS). (C) Linux-based DC OS for Nexus (VDCs, per-process restart, NX-API). Which mapping?
options: (empty) — no
Identical — false
(empty) — no
IOS-XE = enterprise modular IOS (ASR/ISR/Cat9k, Linux-kernel); IOS-XR = carrier-grade HA SP OS (ASR9k/NCS); NX-OS = DC OS for Nexus (VDCs, per-process restart)
questions.explanation: IOS-XE: enterprise campus/WAN (ISR, ASR 1000, Catalyst). IOS-XR: service provider (ASR 9000, CRS, NCS) — microkernel, process isolation, ISSU. NX-OS: Nexus data center switches — Python API, vPC, FabricPath.

questions.question: An LACP-bundled port-channel between two switches uses default LACP timers — PDUs every 30 s, detect partner failure in 90 s. The team wants FASTER member-failure detection. The LACP rate flag SLOW → FAST cuts PDUs to every 1 s and detection to ~3 s. Which describes LACP rate fast?
options: Increases bandwidth — false; bandwidth is set by member count
LACP rate fast: changes PDU interval from 30 s (slow) to 1 s (fast); detects link/partner failure within ~3 s instead of ~90 s
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: LACP timers: slow = 30s PDUs, timeout 90s. Fast = 1s PDUs, timeout 3s. Fast mode increases failover speed at the cost of slightly more control traffic. 'channel-group X mode active; lacp rate fast'.

questions.question: BGP allows tagging routes with 32-bit values that other ASes can match on to apply policy. Well-known examples: NO_EXPORT (don't advertise outside this AS), NO_ADVERTISE (don't tell ANY peer), customer-tagged values like 65000:100. The values are transitive optional attributes. What is this BGP feature?
options: (empty) — no
(empty) — no
BGP Communities — 32-bit transitive optional attributes tagging routes for policy use; well-known values: NO_EXPORT, NO_ADVERTISE, NO_PEER; custom private values used by ISPs and enterprises
BGP AS number type — wrong concept
questions.explanation: Communities tag routes for policy. Example: ISP might accept 65000:100 to request lower local preference (deprioritize path). Well-known: NO_EXPORT (FFFF:FF01), NO_ADVERTISE (FFFF:FF02), INTERNET (0:0).

questions.question: OSPF can redistribute external routes (from EIGRP / BGP / static) into the OSPF domain in TWO metric flavours. (E1) external metric ACCUMULATES the internal OSPF cost as the route traverses OSPF — different OSPF routers may pick different best paths to the same external. (E2) external metric is FIXED at the boundary — all OSPF routers see the same metric regardless of path length to the ASBR. Which mapping?
options: E1 = external cost + internal OSPF cost (grows with path length); E2 = external cost only (fixed; same value at every OSPF router regardless of distance to the ASBR)
Always select the same paths — false; they differ
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: E2 (default): cost stays constant across the OSPF domain — all routers see same external cost. E1: cost increases as packet traverses OSPF — allows best exit point selection when multiple ASBRs advertise same external route.

questions.question: Cisco's enterprise NAC platform provides: 802.1X auth + EAP, MAB (MAC Auth Bypass for non-auth-capable devices), device profiling (DHCP fingerprints + active probes), posture assessment (AV up to date? Patches?), and TrustSec policy push (SGT assignment). Which product?
options: (empty) — no
Cisco ISE (Identity Services Engine) — 802.1X auth + MAB + profiling + posture assessment + TrustSec SGT assignment; central NAC + AAA platform
(empty) — no
VPN concentrator — wrong category (that's ASA / Firepower)
questions.explanation: ISE: RADIUS/TACACS+ server + NAC + policy engine. Authenticates users/devices (Active Directory, certificates), profiles device type, checks posture (antivirus, patch level), assigns SGTs and VLANs dynamically.

questions.question: Cisco NSO is a MULTI-VENDOR orchestration platform with: YANG service models, NEDs (Network Element Drivers) that translate service models to per-device configs, atomic service commits across many devices, network-wide rollback, REST + CLI + Python APIs. Which describes NSO?
options: Hardware switch — false
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
Cisco NSO (Network Services Orchestrator) — YANG service-model orchestration with multi-vendor NEDs, atomic service commits, network-wide rollback, multi-vendor via vendor NEDs
questions.explanation: NSO uses service-to-device abstraction with NEDs (Network Element Drivers) for each vendor. Service templates generate device-specific configs. Transactional commits ensure all-or-nothing configuration changes.

questions.question: Network automation needs VENDOR-NEUTRAL DATA MODELS describing device configuration + state. The IETF picked a DOMAIN-SPECIFIC modelling language similar to XML Schema but human-readable. Models are used by NETCONF / RESTCONF / gNMI as the payload schema. Which language?
options: Python library — false; YANG is a modelling language, not a library
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
YANG (RFC 6020) — Yet Another Next Generation; data modelling language for NETCONF / RESTCONF / gNMI; vendor-neutral config + state schemas (OpenConfig, IETF, Cisco-IOS-XE-native)
questions.explanation: YANG models define what can be configured/read on a device. Example: ietf-interfaces YANG model describes interface config. Tools: pyang (validator), netmiko (CLI), ncclient (NETCONF). Cisco IOS-XE supports YANG natively. a data modeling language (RFC 6020) that defines the structure and semantics of network device configuration and state data, used with NETCONF and RESTCONF protocols.

questions.question: An OSPF Autonomous System Boundary Router (ASBR) redistributes EXTERNAL routes (from EIGRP / BGP / RIP / static) into the OSPF AS. These routes are flooded throughout the AS — across area boundaries — as a SPECIFIC LSA type. Which?
options: Type 5 External LSA — originated by ASBRs to advertise external (redistributed) routes throughout the OSPF AS; flooded across area boundaries (except into stub areas)
(empty) — no
Intra-area LSA — that's Type 1/2; Type 5 is external and AS-wide
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: ASBR generates Type 5 LSAs for redistributed external routes. These flood everywhere except stub areas (which block Type 5/4). Totally Stubby: blocks Type 3,4,5 (only default route). NSSA uses Type 7 converted to Type 5 at ABR.

questions.question: Cisco's older SDN controller (APIC-EM) was deprecated in 2019. Its successor (now renamed Catalyst Center) extends to Intent-Based Networking: device design + provisioning + ML-driven assurance + group-based policy. Which mapping?
options: Same product — false
(empty) — no
APIC-EM = older SDN controller (deprecated 2019); DNA Center (now Catalyst Center) = successor with IBN: design, provisioning, ML-based assurance, group-based policy
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: APIC-EM (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller - Enterprise Module) was Cisco's first campus SDN controller. DNA Center supersedes it with: SD-Access fabric management, Assurance analytics, automation at scale.

questions.question: Two BGP policy tools: (A) a SIMPLE ordered list that only MATCHES IP prefixes + mask-length range (`permit 10.0.0.0/8 le 24`). Fast, efficient, deny-by-default. (B) A POWERFUL ordered-rule construct that can MATCH on AS-path, prefix, community, metric, neighbor, AND SET attributes (local-pref, MED, weight, community, next-hop). Which?
options: (empty) — no
(empty) — no
Identical — false

Prefix list = ordered list matching prefix + length range only (fast filter); Route map = ordered match-and-set construct with rich match (AS-path / community / metric / neighbor) AND set (local-pref / MED / weight / community / next-hop)
questions.explanation: Prefix lists are faster than ACLs for IP prefix matching. Route maps use match/set clauses for full policy control. Example: route map to set local preference for routes matching a specific prefix list. Applied to BGP neighbors.

questions.question: Two OSPF routers on the same segment need to DISCOVER each other and verify the neighbour is still alive. Periodic packets every 10 s (broadcast / P2P) carry: router-id, area-id, Hello/Dead intervals, DR/BDR addresses, network mask, authentication. Both ends MUST AGREE on Hello interval, Dead interval, area, mask, authentication for adjacency. Which packet?
options: (empty) — no
OSPF Hello packets — discover and maintain neighbour adjacency; carry router-id, area-id, timers, DR/BDR, mask, auth; both sides must match these for FULL adjacency
Exchange routing tables — that's DBD / LSU during exchange/loading, not Hello
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: OSPF Hellos are sent every 10s (broadcast/P2P) or 30s (NBMA) to 224.0.0.5. After Dead interval (4× Hello) without a Hello, the neighbor is declared down. Mismatch in Hello/Dead, area, stub flag, or auth = no adjacency.

questions.question: Two tenants share ONE physical router but must have ISOLATED routing tables — including OVERLAPPING IP space (both use 10.0.0.0/8). The router provides per-tenant RIB / FIB / interfaces / routing-protocol instances inside ONE chassis. Which technology?
options: Virtual RAM Forwarding — not a real term
(empty) — no
(empty) — no
VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding) — multiple isolated routing tables on one router; supports overlapping IP space; used by MPLS L3VPN per-customer VRFs
questions.explanation: VRFs partition the routing table: each VRF has its own RIB, FIB, and interfaces. Used in: MPLS L3 VPN (PE router has per-customer VRF), network device management (Mgmt VRF), overlapping address spaces.

questions.question: Branch users on roaming laptops need protection from malicious domains BEFORE the TCP connection is established. A cloud DNS resolver blocks lookups for known-bad domains, malware C2, phishing sites — at the DNS layer. Which Cisco product?
options: Cisco Umbrella — cloud-delivered DNS-layer security; blocks malicious domains / IPs at resolution time before the TCP handshake
(empty) — no
A VPN service — different category (Umbrella ≠ VPN)
(empty) — no
questions.explanation: Umbrella uses Cisco Talos intelligence to block malicious domains via DNS. All DNS queries routed through Umbrella resolvers. Provides: web filtering, malware blocking, DNS-layer security, and cloud-delivered CASB/SIG capabilities.

questions.question: A SecOps team wants behavioural anomaly detection across the network — insider threat, C2, data exfiltration patterns — by analysing NetFlow / IPFIX records over time. The platform applies ML / behavioural baselines to flag anomalies. Which Cisco product?
options: (empty) — no
(empty) — no
A firewall — different category
Cisco Stealthwatch / Secure Network Analytics — ingests NetFlow / IPFIX, applies ML / behavioural baselines to detect insider threats, malware, exfil
questions.explanation: Stealthwatch correlates flow data from routers, switches, firewalls. Detects: slow data exfiltration (beaconing), ransomware spread, compromised hosts (C2 communication), DDoS, policy violations. No agents required.

questions.question: Encrypted traffic can't be content-inspected without DECRYPTION (which is expensive + ethically contentious). Cisco's solution analyses METADATA — packet size patterns, TLS fingerprints (JA3), inter-packet timing, sequence of packet lengths — to detect malware C2 in TLS without decrypting. Which technology?
options: Decryption technology — opposite; ETA avoids decryption
